justice: The entire narrow concrete passage is dominated by vehicle priority, with almost no dedicated exclusive space reserved for pedestrian travel.
There is a complete absence of tactile paving, barrier-free curb cuts and accessibility facilities, severely limiting independent travel access for elderly and disabled residents.
No equitable spatial allocation exists for vulnerable groups, resulting in unfair right-of-way distribution across different road users.
safety: The single narrow lane supports full mixed traffic of pedestrians, bicycles and motor vehicles with no physical separation, raising collision risks.
No traffic calming markings, crosswalks or speed reduction measures are set along the straight residential alley.
Overhead dense power lines and utility poles create potential overhead hazards, with poor emergency evacuation space available.
livability: Basic roadside greenery provides limited natural atmosphere for the residential street environment.
Zero public rest benches, outdoor activity facilities or community gathering amenities are provided along the route.
Low street vitality and limited natural surveillance reduce the sense of personal safety for residents during off-peak hours.
sustainability: Fixed roadside shrubs and greenery deliver minor ecological carbon sequestration and heat mitigation benefits.
No low-carbon travel priority design discourages walking and cycling trips, maintaining reliance on private motorized transport.
Impermeable full concrete pavement lacks sponge city rainwater infiltration and sustainable stormwater management functions.
aesthetics: Traditional village architecture with white walls and black tiles creates a simple, neat rural street visual characteristic.
Exposed overhead wires and dense utility pole arrangement severely clutter the upper street skyline.
Unfinished wall surfaces and scattered roadside debris reduce the overall tidiness and visual coherence of the streetscape.
comfort: Side vegetation offers partial sun shading and creates a relatively quiet rural ambient environment.
No pedestrian buffer zones exist; pedestrians must travel very close to oncoming vehicles, bringing obvious psychological discomfort.
Zero resting facilities along the long straight route create significant physical fatigue risk for elderly walkers.
walkability: There is no separated dedicated sidewalk; pedestrians must share the same narrow lane with all motorized traffic.
Lack of accessible design, crossing points and pedestrian priority design makes daily foot travel inconvenient and high-risk.
Monotonous enclosed street layout provides little visual attraction and greatly discourages active walking behaviour.
bikeability: No designated bicycle lane or cycling exclusive space is reserved on this narrow residential alley.
Full mixed traffic environment with no lane separation creates an intimidating and unsafe experience for all cyclists.
Complete lack of bicycle parking facilities and cycling guidance signage makes daily cycling highly impractical.
